scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being AITA (A Guy in Trouble) for refusing to pump my girlfriend's tire. Let me start by understanding the situation better. From what I gather, whenever my girlfriend has any car maintenance issues, she tends to hold me accountable for fixing them or taking care of them. That seems a bit one-sided, but I can see how she might expect help from her partner. A while back, her tire had an issue, and I was the first to notice it was low. I gave her a heads-up before she left for work. A day later, the tire was completely flat because she didn't pump air into it or get it inspected. So, I ended up fixing it for her. At that time, I also bought her a PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. That was about the extent of my car-fixing skills, and I made it clear that I don't know much about cars beyond the basics like changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, and jump-starting. Despite my limitations, she insisted that I call her dad or watch YouTube videos to learn more about car maintenance. My response was that I'd prefer a mechanic handle it and that she could learn to do these things herself if she wanted. Now, another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two. She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive to the gas station to fill the tire as needed until she gets it fixed or replaced. She claims she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. I asked her why she needed strangers (who are always men, by the way) to do something I've already taught her how to do. She said she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately, it's a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner, regardless of gender, you should know how to do something as basic as pumping a tire and changing a flat (especially since I showed her how). I also mentioned that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in Distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. She replied that all her male friends and family agreed with her and that they were "real men" because they knew how to take care of a woman. I don't really care for these outdated gender roles and have made that very clear. On top of that, I do plenty of handywork around the house, cook and clean regularly (I cook more often than she does, in fact), and I pay the majority of our expenses, including all of her rent. The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards or stereotype expectations just because she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing that to me. To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused. Now, I'm determined not to lift a finger. Am I AITA here? Okay, so I need to figure out whether refusing to pump her tire in this situation is AITA or not. Let's break it down step by step. First, I need to understand what AITA means. From what I know, AITA is a term used to describe a situation where a man is being overly accommodating or going out of his way to help his partner, often to the point of being taken advantage of or put in a difficult position. In this case, I'm refusing to pump her tire, which she's asking me to do. So, is refusing to help her in this situation AITA? Or is it justified given the circumstances? Let's consider the dynamics of the relationship. She tends to hold me accountable for fixing her car issues, which seems like a lot to ask of someone who doesn't know much about cars. I've already shown her how to use a PSI gauge and pump air into the tire. She claims she doesn't know how to do it, but I've taught her. She also insists that it's a man's responsibility to handle such tasks, which I find outdated and unfair. I do plenty of other things around the house and contribute financially, so I don't see why I should be the one to handle all the car maintenance as well. Moreover, she's comfortable relying on strangers to help her with these tasks, which seems risky and impractical. I've offered to teach her again, but she refused. Given all this, I'm deciding not to help her with pumping the tire anymore. Is that AITA? Or is it a reasonable decision given the circumstances? I think it's important to consider the balance of responsibilities in a relationship. Both partners should ideally contribute to maintaining their shared responsibilities, whether it's household chores, financial contributions, or car maintenance. In this case, I've already taken the initiative to teach her how to handle basic car maintenance tasks. She's choosing not to learn or take responsibility for her own car issues, which is putting the burden solely on me. Refusing to help her in this situation might be seen as AITA if I'm the one always accommodating her needs without reciprocation. However, in this case, I've already made it clear that I don't have the expertise to handle more complex car issues and that she should consider learning these skills herself or hiring a professional. By refusing to pump her tire, I'm setting boundaries to ensure that responsibilities are shared fairly in our relationship. It's not about being unhelpful or uncaring; it's about establishing a healthy balance where both partners contribute to maintaining their shared life. Therefore, I don't think refusing to pump her tire in this situation is AITA. It's a reasonable decision to set boundaries and encourage mutual responsibility in the relationship.
